title: Many Reformed oppose liberty only to compulsion and define it as freedom from compulsion
source_text: IV. Verum non explicant omnes eodem modo qua in re sita sit libertas, ratione cujus homo liber in agendo dicitur, & a qua denominatur liberum ejus arbitrium. Et primo quidem ex Reformatis non pauci, libertatem illam cujus respectu homo dicitur esse liberi arbitrii, nec servituti, nec necessitati simpliciter opponi docent, sed potius coactioni. Ac plerumque loquuntur quasi coactio sola libertatem perimeret, & libertatem describunt immunitatem a coactione.
pass_a_gloss: But not all explain in the same way in what thing liberty is situated, by reason of which man is said to be free in acting, and from which his choice is called free. And first indeed not a few of the Reformed teach that that liberty in respect of which man is said to be of free choice, is opposed neither to servitude, nor simply to necessity, but rather to coaction. And for the most part they speak as though coaction alone destroyed liberty, and they describe liberty as immunity from coaction.
pass_b_english: They do not all explain in the same way what the freedom consists in that makes man free in acting and gives his choice the name free.

To begin with, a good many of the Reformed teach that the freedom by which man is said to have free choice is not set against bondage, or against necessity as such, but against compulsion. They mostly talk as if compulsion were the only thing that destroys freedom, and they describe freedom as exemption from compulsion.

choices.why: Coactio is force applied against an agent's own inclination; 'compulsion' renders the technical sense.
